title: Parents value home libraries, but cost, time, cultural fit and work strain make household literacy uneven
source_unit: Capita and Book Harvest, More Books for American Families: National Children’s Book Ownership Survey, September 22, 2026
geography: United States; parents and guardians of children ages 0-12, with income, race, reading-routine and cultural-fit comparisons

denominator.unit: U.S. parents and guardians of children ages 0-12 in a national YouGov survey

low_book_supply.unit: percent of families with 10 or fewer children’s books at home

parent_belief.unit: percent of parents saying books at home help children succeed in school

book_ownership_importance.unit: percent saying it matters whether children own their own books rather than only borrow them

observations.method: National YouGov survey conducted for Book Harvest and Capita, balanced by age, gender, race, region, income and political affiliation; reported margin of error ±1.6 percentage points.
observations.uncertainty: This is a partner-sponsored survey and the public brief does not establish causal effects of book ownership on educational or civic outcomes; household book counts and beliefs are self-reported.
observations.subgroup: Parents and guardians of children ages 0-12 across U.S. households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Book counts alone do not measure reading quality, library access, digital reading, language development or the home relationships that make books useful; a small library can still be actively used.

observations.period: May 7-June 1, 2026; unequal household book access by race and income

denominator.unit: U.S. parents and guardians of children ages 0-12; subgroup estimates use their weighted universes

black_low_supply.unit: percent of Black families with 10 or fewer children’s books at home

hispanic_low_supply.unit: percent of Hispanic families with 10 or fewer children’s books at home

white_low_supply.unit: percent of White families with 10 or fewer children’s books at home

low_income_low_supply.unit: percent of families earning under $30,000 with 10 or fewer children’s books, versus 19% among families earning $100,000 or more

observations.method: YouGov cross-tabulation of reported home book ownership by race and household income.
observations.uncertainty: The public brief does not provide all subgroup sample sizes or confidence intervals; race and income are associated with book supply but do not identify the mechanisms or household preferences.
observations.subgroup: Black, Hispanic and White families and households below $30,000 versus at least $100,000 annual income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unequal home collections may reflect price, access to culturally relevant books, housing space, gifting networks, local institutions, language, or differences in how families define children’s books—not income alone.

observations.period: May 7-June 1, 2026; cultural fit and cost as barriers to home libraries

denominator.unit: U.S. parents and guardians of children ages 0-12; subgroup estimates use their weighted universes

book_cost_barrier.unit: percent of parents saying cost of books is a barrier; 65% among families under $30,000 and 41% among families at least $100,000

cultural_fit_hispanic.unit: percent of Hispanic families reporting difficulty finding books reflecting their culture, language or identity

cultural_fit_black.unit: percent of Black families reporting difficulty finding books reflecting their culture, language or identity

cultural_fit_white.unit: percent of White families reporting the same difficulty

observations.method: YouGov survey questions on book cost and the availability of books matching children’s culture, language and identity.
observations.uncertainty: Barrier reports capture perceived availability and affordability, not local retail prices, library holdings, translation supply or actual search behavior.
observations.subgroup: Families by income and race/ethnicity, including Hispanic, Black and White families.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cultural fit is only one dimension of book selection; families may value plot, developmental level, author, format, language learning and child preference simultaneously.

observations.period: May 7-June 1, 2026; household time and work conditions around reading

denominator.unit: U.S. parents and guardians of children ages 0-12; reading-routine estimates use their relevant weighted universe

daily_reading.unit: percent reading aloud with children every day; 17% read five to six times a week and 25% two to four times a week

rare_or_never.unit: percent rarely or never reading aloud

work_responsibility_barrier.unit: percent pointing to work and other responsibilities as a reason they cannot read as often as desired

fatigue_barrier.unit: percent citing fatigue as a barrier

observations.method: YouGov survey of reading frequency and reasons parents report reading less often than they would like.
observations.uncertainty: Reading frequency and reasons are self-reported and do not establish whether work schedules, fatigue, book access, child preference or other factors cause the routine gap.
observations.subgroup: Parents and guardians of children ages 0-12, with comparisons by income and race reported in the brief.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reading aloud is one form of literacy practice; it does not capture independent reading, storytelling, school support, audio books or other family learning activities.

related_sources.claim: Book Harvest is the partner organization conducting the annual National Children’s Book Ownership Survey with Capita.

boundary: This record treats home book ownership and reading routines as a household cultural-access mechanism linking cost, time, race, language, identity, work schedules and civic capacity. It does not establish that book counts cause educational or democratic outcomes, define a sufficient home library, or replace libraries, schools, digital resources and relational learning.
